concepts.title: What Makes Writing Creative
concepts.definition: Creative writing is writing that imaginatively transforms experience -- stories, poems, plays -- rather than reporting it. Its material is the same world we all see, but reshaped through a personal vision, and its aim is effect on a reader: delight, suspense, sorrow or laughter.
concepts.key_idea: Report tells what happened; creation tells what it felt like -- imagination recasting experience for effect.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb116.txt opening (shakespeare lines from macbeth as description, imaginative writing versus reporting, effect on the reader)
question_patterns: what distinguishes creative writing from ordinary writing
in class 11 creative writing: how does imagination transform experience
why does the chapter open with lines from macbeth
what effects can creative writing produce in a reader
distinguish reporting an event from narrating it imaginatively
is a diary entry creative writing discuss

solution_steps.explain: A police report records; a story re-imagines -- selecting, exaggerating, ordering for effect.
Vivid images, telling detail, rhythm and point of view carry the writer's vision.
Creative writing succeeds when the reader feels something -- the aim is experience transferred.

concepts.title: Elements of a Story: Plot, Character, Setting
concepts.definition: A short story stands on three supports: plot, the linked sequence of events rising to a climax and ending in resolution; character, people whose wants and changes drive the events; and setting, the time and place that clothe both in atmosphere.
concepts.key_idea: Someone (character) wants something, events (plot) push against the want, and a place (setting) holds it all.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb116.txt story sections (plot and its development, characters and their motives, setting and atmosphere, climax and resolution)
question_patterns: explain the elements of a short story
in class 11 creative writing: what is the role of conflict in a plot
how does setting create atmosphere in a story
distinguish flat characters from rounded characters
plan a short story using plot character and setting
what makes a satisfying ending to a story

solution_steps.explain: Give a character a want, block it, and let events rise through complications to a climax and some resolution.
Show characters through speech, act and motive so readers can believe and care.
Choose time and place details that reinforce the mood and make events credible.

concepts.title: Language of Imagination: Figures of Speech and Point of View
concepts.definition: Creative power lives in language: similes and metaphors compare and compress, personification wakes the inert, and choosing a point of view -- first person or third -- decides whose eyes the reader borrows. Precise, sensory words outdo piles of adjectives.
concepts.key_idea: See through one pair of eyes, name things exactly, compare boldly -- that is the language of imagination.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb116.txt language sections (simile metaphor personification, sensory words, point of view first person third person, avoiding cliches)
question_patterns: explain simile metaphor and personification with examples
in class 11 creative writing: how does point of view change a story
why are sensory words preferred to strings of adjectives
identify the figures of speech in a given passage
retell an event in first person and in third person
how can cliches be replaced with fresh images

solution_steps.explain: Decide who tells the tale; first person offers intimacy, third person offers breadth.
Deploy simile, metaphor and personification sparingly but freshly to compress meaning into images.
Select exact nouns and verbs that appeal to the senses, cutting worn-out phrases.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Plan a two-paragraph story about a lost puppy using plot, character and setting.

solution_template.explain: A small boy wants to find the puppy that followed him home -- motive established.
Searching streets, a scare, then reunion with its owner -- complication, climax, resolution.
A rainy evening market gives atmosphere: smells, umbrellas, dim lantern light.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Rewrite the flat sentence 'The old house was very scary at night' using a figure of speech and sensory detail.

solution_template.explain: Personification: 'The old house held its breath at night.'
Sound and touch: 'floorboards groaned, and the cold staircase rail felt like a bone under the hand.'
The rewrite shows the scare instead of announcing it -- concrete images outperform the vague adjective.
